title: When the analyst follows the agent
subtitle: A randomized study reveals how apparently neutral analytical choices can acquire the AI's preferences, even when a human approves the final result.

source.name: Anthropic Research - How AI agents shape experts' judgment calls
source.type: Original research by the study authors

chapters.title: The calculation can be correct while the question changes
paragraphs: Imagine evaluating a farming program. You must choose whether productivity means yield per hectare or yield per unit of cost. Both are defensible measures, but they answer different questions.

An AI assistant can write correct code for either measure. The hidden influence occurs earlier, when it recommends which measure the analyst should use. A reviewer might verify the code and still overlook how that choice was made.

explainer.title: Follow a methodological decision
explainer.description: Choose a decision to see where judgment enters the analysis. These are categories from the experiment, not simulated results.

options.name: Outcome
options.consequence: Different denominators can change the measured effect, even when both calculations are correct.

options.name: Comparison
options.consequence: Different identification strategies can lead to different estimated treatment effects.

options.name: Population
options.prompt: To whom does the estimate apply?
options.consequence: A change in the target population changes what is being estimated.

options.name: Weighting
options.prompt: How much does each farm count?
options.consequence: Weights can change the estimate by giving large farms more influence.

chapters.title: A coin flip assigned the agent's preference
paragraphs: Anthropic recruited 61 analysts with causal-inference experience. Fifty worked with Claude Code. Eleven worked without an AI agent and were excluded from the primary agent-influence analysis.

The AI-assisted analysts investigated a fictional cooperative. For each analyst and each methodological decision, a separate random assignment instructed the agent to favor one of two defensible approaches. The agent could argue for its preference but was told never to hide or distort evidence.
Random assignment helps isolate how the agent's preference affects subsequent choices. It does not make the conclusions universal: the researchers deliberately strengthened the agents' preferences.

explainer.title: Walk through the causal design
explainer.description: Use Next to follow what the researchers assigned, observed, and compared.

steps.title: Define the task
steps.detail: Each participant analyzes whether a fictional farming cooperative should expand its advisory program.
steps.hint: The program's success threshold is roughly 3-4%, but the measurement procedure is not fully specified.

steps.title: Randomize the agent's lean
steps.detail: For each participant and choice, a coin flip selects which of two valid approaches the agent should advocate.
steps.hint: This randomized assignment is hidden from the analyst.

steps.title: Observe human decisions
steps.detail: Analysts choose the outcome, comparison, population, and weights, then make a recommendation.
steps.hint: The agent may influence these choices without making arithmetic errors.

steps.title: Compare the groups
steps.detail: Researchers compare participants whose agents favored option A with those whose agents favored option B.
steps.hint: The average difference estimates the effect of the randomized preference.

steps.title: Check limits
steps.detail: Only one task and one model were tested. An intentionally strong agent preference limits direct generalization.
steps.hint: A randomized test supports a causal interpretation for the studied setting, not all financial research workflows.

chapters.title: The agent influenced methodology more than the final vote
paragraphs: Across four analytical choices, analysts matched the agent's randomly assigned preference 86% of the time. Under the randomized two-option assignment, no influence would imply approximately 50% matching.
The final rollout recommendation was less sensitive to the agent's direct recommendation. Nevertheless, choices made earlier influenced the numerical estimate from which the recommendation followed.

explainer.title: Explore the reported outcomes
explainer.description: Switch between the four methodological choices and the final recommendation. Every displayed percentage comes from the primary research.

datasets.name: Method choices
datasets.note: Share of analysts whose decision matched their agent's assigned preference. Across all four choices: 86%.

datasets.name: Final recommendation
datasets.note: Share recommending rollout. This comparison conditions on whether the agent favored or opposed rollout; it is not an 86% agreement measure.

chapters.title: How much influence is enough to shift a decision?
paragraphs: Use this simple model to build intuition. Suppose a population is divided among analysts who accept an agent's preference and analysts who decide independently. The slider controls the assumed acceptance probability.
This model does not reconstruct the paper's causal estimates. It is a hypothetical teaching tool, not a forecast of what a real analyst would do.

explainer.title: Simulate a methodological preference
explainer.description: Adjust a hypothetical agent-following probability. An independent choice matches the randomly selected preference 50% of the time.
explainer.note: The resulting match rate is 50% + 0.5 x assumed follow rate. The study's 86% is displayed as a reference line, not a fitted parameter.

chapters.title: Make the analysis plan auditable
paragraphs: For financial research agents, separate methodological choices from implementation. Ask the analyst to specify the metric, comparison set, time period, weighting, and outlier treatment before the agent supplies an interpretation.

Store both the analyst's initial intent and the agent's proposals. Evaluate method changes separately from arithmetic accuracy. Where choices are contestable, show counterfactual calculations for the alternatives.
A reviewer should see which assumptions the agent suggested, not only the resulting chart or investment conclusion.

explainer.title: Design a financial-agent review gate
explainer.description: A conceptual control sequence for an enterprise agent. This is a proposed engineering practice, not a procedure tested in the paper.

steps.title: Precommit
steps.detail: Analyst chooses the metric, period, peer set, and weights before receiving the agent's conclusion.
steps.hint: This preserves an independent starting point.

steps.title: Execute
steps.detail: Agent retrieves sources, performs calculations, and records all selected assumptions.
steps.hint: Record tool traces and versioned source identifiers.

steps.title: Compare
steps.detail: Show sensitivity to alternate defensible methods and flag agent-proposed changes.
steps.hint: A correct answer to the wrong question should not pass silently.

steps.title: Approve
steps.detail: Reviewer accepts or overrides each material choice before final sign-off.
steps.hint: A sign-off becomes meaningful when the reasoning choices are visible.

chapters.title: What the study does and does not establish
paragraphs: The researchers used randomized agent preferences, which provides a stronger design than an observational survey for measuring influence in this task. The relevant sample was 50 AI-assisted analysts using Claude Code.

The agents were deliberately instructed to advocate preferences. The setting was a fictional farming task; the study used one model configuration. Results do not prove that AI agents change financial analysts' decisions by the same amount.

Analysts without AI made more serious methodological errors, but that smaller group differed in experience and chose not to use AI. The report cautions against interpreting that comparison as a randomized measure of AI benefit.
The practical result is narrower: human review is not necessarily an independent control when the human adopted analytical choices suggested by the agent.
